name: Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater)
why: An iron meteorite about 50 metres across struck here roughly 50,000 years ago. The bowl is about 1.2 km wide, and the raised, blocky rim is rock thrown out by the blast.

name: Manicouagan Reservoir
why: A ring of water around a central island marks an impact about 214 million years ago. Erosion wore the crater down, and a dam flooded the ring that remains.

name: Richat Structure (the Eye of the Sahara)
why: Its rings were once taken for an impact crater. Geologists now read them as a dome of layered rock, pushed up and then worn flat, so the hard and soft layers show as circles.

name: Wadi As-Sirhan farms
why: Each green disc is a field watered by a centre-pivot sprinkler, a long arm turning around a well. The water is ancient groundwater, pumped up from deep aquifers under the desert.

name: Kufra farms
why: Circles of crops in the open Sahara near the Kufra oasis, each watered by a centre-pivot sprinkler drawing on the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, water laid down when the region was wetter.

name: Mississippi River Delta
why: The river runs out into the Gulf between thin levees of its own mud, splitting into channels like the toes of a bird's foot. Sediment plumes show where it drops its load.

name: Betsiboka River delta
why: The river runs rust-red with soil washed off the highlands, where forest loss has left the ground bare. It drops that sediment as islands where it meets the sea.

name: Lena Delta
why: One of the largest deltas in the Arctic, a fan of channels and thousands of small lakes on frozen ground. It is free of ice only for a few summer months.

name: Salar de Uyuni
why: The largest salt flat on Earth, the dried floor of a prehistoric lake, crusted with salt metres thick. It is so flat that satellites use it to calibrate their altimeters.

name: Lake Natron
why: A shallow, very salty and alkaline lake. Salt-loving microbes can turn its shallows pink and red, and it is a major breeding ground for lesser flamingos.

name: Lithium ponds, Salar de Atacama
why: Brine pumped from under the salt flat is left in ponds to evaporate in the sun. As it concentrates, the colour shifts, until it is rich enough in lithium to process.

name: Aletsch Glacier
why: The largest glacier in the Alps, a river of ice about 20 km long. The dark stripes are medial moraines, rock carried along where tributary glaciers join.

name: Malaspina Glacier
why: A piedmont glacier: ice spills from the mountains onto flat ground and spreads into a lobe. Surges fold its dark moraines into zigzags.

name: Geirangerfjord
why: A long, steep-sided inlet carved by glaciers in the ice ages and then flooded by the sea when the ice melted.

name: Bingham Canyon Mine
why: One of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world, more than a kilometre deep. The rings are benches, terraces cut so trucks can spiral down.

name: Mir diamond mine
why: A former diamond mine, a pit about 525 metres deep and 1.2 km across, dug into a kimberlite pipe. The town of Mirny sits right beside it.

name: Aldabra Atoll
why: A ring of raised coral limestone around a shallow lagoon, home to about 100,000 giant tortoises. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Palm Jumeirah
why: Built from sand dredged from the sea floor and shaped into a palm tree, with a breakwater crescent around it to keep the waves off.

name: Mount Taranaki
why: A cone-shaped stratovolcano ringed by forest. The almost perfect circle is the national park boundary, where native bush meets farmland.

name: Mount Fuji
why: Japan's highest mountain, an active stratovolcano that last erupted in 1707. Snow outlines the summit crater and the gullies on its slopes.

name: Mount Etna
why: Europe's most active volcano. Dark tongues of younger lava run down its flanks over older, weathered flows and farmland.

name: Sossusvlei dunes
why: Some of the tallest dunes on Earth, red from iron oxide on the sand. Winds from several directions build them into star-shaped ridges.

name: Waimakariri River
why: A wide bed of gravel with many shallow channels that split and rejoin. Rivers braid like this when they carry heavy loads of gravel down from mountains.

name: Ucayali River
why: A lowland river in the Amazon basin that swings in wide loops across its floodplain. Cut-off loops are left behind as crescent-shaped oxbow lakes.

name: Clearwater Lakes
why: Two ring-shaped lakes, each the trace of a meteorite impact. They were long taken for twins from one strike; dating has since shown they formed hundreds of millions of years apart.

name: Lonar Lake
why: A meteorite crater about 1.8 km wide, blasted into the thick basalt of the Deccan Traps. It holds a salty, alkaline lake.

name: Pingualuit Crater
why: A near-perfect circle 3.4 km wide, made by an impact about 1.4 million years ago. Its lake, fed only by rain and snow, is one of the clearest in the world.

name: Wolfe Creek Crater
why: A meteorite crater about 880 metres across in the edge of the Great Sandy Desert, one of the best-preserved on Earth.

name: Gosses Bluff (Tnorala)
why: A ring of hills about 5 km wide: the worn-down core of a crater left by an impact about 142 million years ago. It is a sacred site to the Western Arrernte people.

name: Tengger caldera and Mount Bromo
why: A volcanic caldera about 10 km wide, floored with a 'sea of sand'. New cones, including the smoking Mount Bromo, have grown up inside it.

name: Crater Lake
why: About 7,700 years ago the volcano Mount Mazama erupted and collapsed into itself. Rain and snow filled the hollow, making the deepest lake in the United States.

name: Santorini
why: The ring of islands is the rim of a volcano. A huge eruption about 3,600 years ago emptied its magma chamber, the centre collapsed, and the sea flooded in.

name: Ngorongoro Crater
why: A volcanic caldera about 20 km across, the largest unbroken and unflooded one in the world. Its floor is grassland, a soda lake and home to a dense population of wildlife.

name: Mount Kilimanjaro
why: Africa's highest mountain, a dormant volcano 5,895 m high. The white patches at the summit are the remains of ice fields that have shrunk sharply over the past century.

name: Mount St. Helens
why: In 1980 the north side of the mountain slid away and a sideways blast flattened the forest. The horseshoe-shaped crater still opens to the north.

name: Holuhraun lava field
why: Lava that poured out in 2014–15, covering about 85 km², the largest lava flow in Iceland since the Laki eruption of 1783–84.

name: Nile Delta
why: The Nile fans out north of Cairo before reaching the Mediterranean. The green triangle of fields against the desert holds much of Egypt's farmland and people.

name: Okavango Delta
why: An inland delta: the Okavango River spreads out across the Kalahari and never reaches the sea. Its water soaks in or evaporates, feeding a huge wetland.

name: Sundarbans
why: The largest mangrove forest on Earth, on the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna. Tidal channels thread through it, and it is home to Bengal tigers.

name: Perito Moreno Glacier
why: Its front pushes across Lago Argentino, at times damming one arm of the lake until the water bursts through the ice.

name: Breiðamerkurjökull and Jökulsárlón
why: As this outlet glacier retreated, a lagoon opened in front of it. Icebergs break off the glacier and drift through the lagoon to the sea.

name: Baltoro Glacier
why: About 63 km long, one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions, flowing among Karakoram peaks including K2. Rock debris stripes its surface.

name: Milford Sound (Piopiotahi)
why: Called a sound, but really a fjord: a valley carved by glaciers in the ice ages and flooded by the sea when they melted.

name: Bonneville Salt Flats
why: A dense crust of salt left by the prehistoric Lake Bonneville. It is so flat and hard that land speed records have been set on it.

name: Great Salt Lake
why: A railway causeway built in 1959 cuts the lake in two. The northern arm gets little river water, so it is far saltier, and salt-loving microbes turn it pink.

name: Dead Sea evaporation ponds
why: The Dead Sea's southern basin is now a grid of ponds where sea water evaporates in the sun, leaving potash and other minerals to be harvested.

name: Centre-pivot fields near Garden City
why: Circles of crops, each watered by a sprinkler arm turning around a well. The water comes from the Ogallala Aquifer under the High Plains, being drawn down faster than it refills.

name: Greenhouses of Almería
why: Tens of thousands of hectares of plastic greenhouses, sometimes called the Sea of Plastic. They grow a large share of Europe's winter vegetables.

name: Deforestation in Rondônia
why: Roads cut into the Amazon rainforest, and farms clear land along each side. From above the cleared strips form a fishbone pattern.

name: Chuquicamata mine
why: One of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world, worked for more than a century in the Atacama Desert.

name: Fimiston Open Pit (the Super Pit)
why: A gold mine about 3.5 km long, cut beside the town of Kalgoorlie. The terraced walls let haul trucks drive down into the pit.

name: Garzweiler mine
why: A vast open-pit mine for lignite, or brown coal. Whole villages have been moved out of its way as it advances.

name: Rangiroa
why: One of the largest atolls in the world, a thin ring of coral islets around a lagoon about 80 km long.

name: The World Islands
why: About 300 islands of dredged sand, laid out in the shape of a world map off the coast of Dubai.

name: Rub' al Khali (the Empty Quarter)
place: Liwa, United Arab Emirates (edge of the Rub' al Khali)
why: The Rub' al Khali is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth. At its edge near Liwa, giant dunes stand between flat salt pans called sabkha.

name: Great Sand Dunes
why: The tallest dunes in North America, piled against the Sangre de Cristo Mountains where opposing winds trap sand blown across the valley.

name: Lençóis Maranhenses
why: White dunes by the Atlantic. Rain in the wet season fills the hollows between them with clear blue lagoons that dry out again later in the year.

name: Brahmaputra River at Majuli
why: The Brahmaputra splits into many shifting channels around sandbars. Majuli, inside it, is one of the largest river islands in the world.

name: Grand Canyon
why: Carved by the Colorado River over millions of years, up to about 1.8 km deep. Its walls expose nearly two billion years of rock layers.

name: Three Gorges Dam
why: A concrete dam across the Yangtze, the hydroelectric power station with the largest capacity in the world. The river above it is a reservoir hundreds of kilometres long.

name: Uluru
why: A single huge sandstone rock rising about 348 metres above the plain. It is sacred to the Aṉangu, its traditional owners.

name: Aral Sea
why: Once one of the four largest lakes in the world. From the 1960s its rivers were diverted to irrigate cotton, and it has lost most of its area, leaving a salty desert.

name: Meeting of Waters
why: The dark Rio Negro meets the sandy Rio Solimões. Different speeds, temperatures and densities keep them running side by side for kilometres before they mix.
